Tail index of a heavy-tailed count

Source: R/concentration.R
hill_tail_index.Rd

The Clauset-Shalizi-Newman maximum-likelihood estimator for a discrete power law above a threshold. An exponent near 2 or below means the mean is barely defined and the observed maximum is not informative about the next one, which is the substantive point when a few units dominate a total. Use it on counts per unit (placements per person, incidents per address) to judge whether the largest values are a heavy tail rather than a few outliers, and read ks and reliable before quoting the exponent.

Usage

hill_tail_index(
  x,
  x_min = NULL,
  discrete = TRUE,
  approx = FALSE,
  min_tail = 3L
)

Arguments

x

Numeric vector of positive values, one per unit.

x_min

Numeric scalar or NULL (the default): the threshold at and above which the power law is fitted. A power law is a statement about the tail, so a threshold is required; NULL takes the 50th largest value (which leaves at least 50 observations in the tail), or the minimum if there are fewer than 50 values.

discrete

Logical scalar, default TRUE: whether the quantity is integer-valued. A count is, and then the likelihood maximised is the zeta distribution's, whose normalising constant is a Hurwitz zeta.

approx

Logical scalar, default FALSE. For discrete data, whether to use the closed-form continuity-corrected estimator instead of maximising the exact likelihood. It is much faster and much worse: the correction is an asymptotic approximation in x_min, and at x_min = 1 – where administrative counts start – it returns about 2.0 from data generated with an exponent of 2.5. Off by default for that reason.

min_tail

Integer scalar, default 3: the fewest tail observations for which an estimate is reported at all (values below 2 are raised to 2). Below it there is nothing to estimate from and alpha is NA.

Value

A list with alpha (numeric, the exponent), se (its standard error), x_min (the threshold used), n_tail (integer, the number of values at or above it), ks, reliable (logical) and method (character, the estimator used or why there is no estimate). ks is the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the fitted tail and the data: a large value means the tail is not a power law, whatever alpha came out as. reliable is FALSE when fewer than 50 observations lie in the tail, which is the sample size Clauset, Shalizi and Newman give as the point below which the estimate should not be leaned on – it is reported rather than enforced, because the right response to a short tail is a wider interval, not a refusal.

Details

For a power law \(p(x) \propto x^{-\alpha}\) above \(x_{min}\):

  • discrete data, exact (the default): the log-likelihood of the zeta distribution truncated at \(x_{min}\), \(-n \log \zeta(\alpha, x_{min}) - \alpha \sum \log x_i\), is maximised over \(\alpha\) in \((1.0001, 25)\) with stats::optimize(); \(\zeta\) is hurwitz_zeta(). The standard error comes from the observed information, by a numerical second derivative.

  • continuous data (discrete = FALSE): the Hill estimator \(\hat\alpha = 1 + n / \sum \log(x_i / x_{min})\), with standard error \((\hat\alpha - 1)/\sqrt{n}\).

  • discrete data with approx = TRUE: the same closed form with \(x_{min} - 1/2\) in place of \(x_{min}\).

ks is the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the fitted distribution and the tail, computed once per distinct value so that ties (most counts are ties) are handled correctly.

Only finite positive values of x are used; the rest are dropped silently. When the tail has fewer than min_tail values, or every tail value is the same, alpha is NA and method says why. An estimate at the optimiser's bound is flagged in method and is not reliable. Errors: no positive finite value in x; x_min that is not a single positive number (logical, factor and text are refused); discrete or approx not TRUE or FALSE.

References

Clauset, A., Shalizi, C. R. and Newman, M. E. J. (2009). Power-law distributions in empirical data. SIAM Review 51(4), 661-703. The estimator and its threshold guidance are theirs; the continuity correction they give in closed form is an asymptotic approximation in x_min, which is why the exact likelihood is maximised here instead. (Not in the local corpus; cited from the published paper.)

Examples

# A continuous Pareto tail with exponent 2.5.
set.seed(1)
x <- (1 - stats::runif(5000))^(-1 / 1.5)
round(hill_tail_index(x, x_min = 1, discrete = FALSE)$alpha, 2)
#> [1] 2.49

# A discrete power law, where the exact likelihood is needed: the
# closed-form correction is badly biased at a threshold of one.
k <- 1:10000
p <- k^(-2.5) / sum(k^(-2.5))
set.seed(2)
z <- sample(k, 5000, replace = TRUE, prob = p)
c(exact = round(hill_tail_index(z, x_min = 1)$alpha, 2),
  approx = round(hill_tail_index(z, x_min = 1, approx = TRUE)$alpha, 2))
#>  exact approx 
#>   2.46   2.00 

# A short tail still returns an estimate, marked as not to be leaned
# on, and with a standard error that says the same thing.
short <- hill_tail_index(c(3, 4, 5, 9), x_min = 3)
c(alpha = round(short$alpha, 2), n = short$n_tail,
  reliable = short$reliable)
#>    alpha        n reliable 
#>     2.59     4.00     0.00 

# Below `min_tail` there is nothing to estimate from.
hill_tail_index(c(3, 4), x_min = 3)$alpha
#> [1] NA

# the threshold has to be positive
try(hill_tail_index(z, x_min = 0))
#> Error : `x_min` must be positive
